title: How Neuromorphic Computing Mimics the Human Brain

slides.heading: How Neuromorphic Computing Mimics the Human Brain
slides.body: The next frontier in computing takes its blueprints directly from neuroscience

slides.heading: What Is Neuromorphic Computing?
slides.body: Neuromorphic computing uses chip architectures modeled after the brain's neural networks. Unlike traditional CPUs that process instructions sequentially, these chips process information in parallel streams — just like biological neurons do.

slides.heading: The Problem With Traditional Chips
slides.body: Conventional computers shuttle data back and forth between a processor and memory — a bottleneck called the von Neumann wall. This wastes enormous energy. The human brain performs far more complex tasks using only about 20 watts, the same power as a dim light bulb.

slides.heading: Spiking Neural Networks: The Core Idea
slides.body: Neuromorphic chips use spiking neural networks (SNNs), where artificial neurons only fire electrical pulses when they receive enough input — exactly like real neurons. This event-driven approach means the chip uses energy only when it actually needs to compute.

slides.heading: Intel's Loihi and IBM's TrueNorth
slides.body: Intel's Loihi 2 chip packs over one million programmable neurons and supports on-chip learning. IBM's TrueNorth holds 4,096 processor cores mimicking 1 million neurons. Both chips consume a fraction of the power of a standard GPU for comparable tasks.

slides.heading: Real-World Applications Today
slides.body: Neuromorphic chips are being used for edge AI — running smart sensors, gesture recognition, and robotics without draining a battery. They excel at processing continuous sensory streams like audio, video, and radar in real time with minimal power.

slides.heading: Learning Like a Brain
slides.body: These chips can implement spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), a biological learning rule where synaptic connections strengthen when two neurons fire in close succession. This enables hardware that adapts and learns without being retrained from scratch each time.

slides.heading: Challenges Still to Solve
slides.body: Programming neuromorphic chips requires entirely new software frameworks — traditional code doesn't apply. Scaling to billions of neurons, managing chip-to-chip communication, and benchmarking performance against GPUs remain active research challenges.

slides.heading: The Road Ahead
slides.body: Research teams are integrating memristors — tiny resistors that remember past electrical states — as artificial synapses, pushing energy efficiency even further. By the late 2020s, neuromorphic systems may power autonomous vehicles, medical implants, and always-on AI assistants.

slides.heading: Brain-Inspired. Energy-Efficient. The Future.
slides.body: Neuromorphic computing won't replace traditional chips — but for tasks requiring real-time sensing and adaptation on minimal power, it may be the most transformative computing shift since the microprocessor.
